text: This tool promises one thing. It formats JSON.
Now watch what it does the moment an agent calls it. It opens your AWS keys. Then your GitHub token. And it tries to ship them to a server it never mentioned.
Most agents would have installed it without a second look. We're Team Spartans, and this is Tool Quarantine.

AI agents now install tools from strangers. You approve a one-line description, not the code. Yet that code runs with your files, your SSH keys, your cloud credentials and your network. We check the promise before you trust it.

cap: How it works: a sealed box on Vultr
text: Each tool runs in a disposable sandbox on a Vultr VM. There is no route to the internet, the disk is read-only, every capability is dropped, and decoy credentials are planted. An agent on Vultr Serverless Inference reads the tool's own description and uses it like a real user, while strace records every file and process, and a sinkhole answers every DNS and HTTP request.

cap: Seven sample MCP servers. All of them look harmless.
text: Here are seven sample MCP servers. From their descriptions, they all look harmless, and each bad one uses a technique seen in real supply chain attacks. Let's quarantine json formatter. It says it does pure formatting.

cap: Live: every file it opens and every host it calls
text: The run starts in a fresh box and streams live. The agent plans a call to format some JSON. Then the tool reads the AWS credentials and the GitHub token, and tries to send them to an analytics host. The sinkhole answers, and keeps the stolen payload as evidence.
Verdict: dangerous, zero out of a hundred. Credential theft and exfiltration are blocking rules in this workspace, so the policy engine blocked this version on its own. Then the box was destroyed.

cap: Blast radius: every reach stopped at the sandbox wall
text: The blast radius shows everything the tool reached for, and where the sandbox wall stopped it. Zero bytes, files or hosts got out.
Claims versus reality puts the tool's own words next to what it actually did. It said pure formatting. It read your credentials. That gap is the signal a static scanner can't see.

cap: Approval is enforced, not a label
text: Approval here is enforced, not a label. Every decision is pinned to a SHA-256 fingerprint of the code, and policy forbids approving this one. Any agent or MCP gateway that asks the registry is refused.

cap: An honest tool, started from the command palette
text: Now an honest tool. I'll start it from the command palette. Unit converter. Pure computation.

cap: TRUSTED 100/100 · approval pins this exact code
text: Trusted, a hundred out of a hundred, nothing touched. I approve it, and that exact code is pinned to the allowlist. If a single byte changes, the fingerprint changes and it has to be quarantined again, so a later update can't sneak in a rug pull.

cap: The registry: every version, pinned by fingerprint
text: The registry lists every approved and blocked version by its fingerprint. This is what gateways, agent runtimes and CI ask before they launch a tool.

cap: Workspace policies with an impact preview
text: Workspace policies decide what gets blocked automatically and what needs a written reason. Change a rule, and the impact preview shows what it would do to your tools before you save.

cap: Drop-in checks for MCP gateways, the CLI and GitHub Actions
text: Integrations are copy and paste: one HTTP call for an MCP gateway, a CLI check that fails for unapproved code, and a GitHub Actions gate.

text: And the overview shows every tool your team has quarantined: threats contained, exfiltration attempts sinkholed, and what is still waiting for a decision.
